finding: At 1× Geth is ~3.3× slower from a single NM peer. At 3.5× the trade-off flips two ways: NM finishes ~4 h sooner (it drains the storage-spam mega-tries as a clean final phase, while Geth front-loads them and stalls stop-go on each one), but Geth is far leaner on memory (~6.7 GB peak vs NM's ~18.4 GB). 5× NM → NM completes in ~17 h over the cross-VM link, ~1.6 TB on disk and ~26 GB RSS — same shape, the storage-spam mega-tries dominating the tail. Every run reconstructs the source state root bit-for-bit.
geth5x: 5× NM → Geth (loopback, single peer) settles at a steady 2.38M slots/min, giving a 'normal' full-sync estimate of ~57 h (~2.4 days) for the 7.79B slots — bound by single-peer request concurrency, not hardware (the box sat ~80% idle). Stock Nethermind couldn't even serve the x5 chain over devp2p until nethermind#12059: 8-billion-gas blocks make 26–47 MB bodies that overflow the 16 MB devp2p limit and desync the RLPx framer; the fix added an accurate size estimator + a 15 MB outgoing-bodies cap (0 framing errors across the ~2-day sync).
caveat: Wall time and bandwidth are single-dedicated-peer, controlled-LAN figures — read as relative scaling across state sizes, not real-world multi-peer sync time. DB size and peak RSS are topology-independent. Source states are frozen; NM uses the additive Sync.StaticSnapPivot flag (nethermind#11943), Geth a minimal fake-CL forkchoice. The 5× NM → Geth wall-time is a steady-state estimate (snapshot-gen still finishing); 7× / 10× snap-sync pending (issues #17 / #18).
